name: tolerant-reader
intent: Keep a consumer working as its producer evolves by reading only the elements it needs, supplying explicit defaults for what is absent, and ignoring every field it does not know.
problem: A consumer that binds a whole payload to a rigid schema breaks when the producer adds a field: code-generated classes from an XSD/WSDL, strict deserialisers and full-document schema validation all reject data that is meant to be backward compatible. The consumer's real dependency - the handful of fields it actually reads - stays implicit, so provider evolution becomes a breaking change by accident instead of by contract.
context: Any producer/consumer seam where the two sides are deployed independently and payloads evolve additively: partner or public APIs, messages on a shared bus, documents persisted by older program versions, SDKs and mobile clients that lag behind the server. The consumer's language should offer name-keyed (schema-less) or forward-compatible (generated-code) deserialisation so undeclared data can simply be skipped, and the cost of ignoring a field must be lower than the cost of breaking on it.
benefits: The producer can add fields without touching or redeploying consumers, so additive evolution stops being a breaking change.
The consumer's true dependency surface becomes explicit and small: the fields it reads and the defaults it applies, instead of the entire payload schema.
Removes the regenerate-and-redeploy treadmill of schema-driven binding (classes generated from XSD/WSDL) and the false sense of safety it creates.
Coupling is confined to the consumed subset, so unrelated producer changes cannot reach application code through the payload type.
Enables consumer-driven contracts: shipping the reader and its tests to the producer turns "what breaks me" into an executable, reviewable artefact.
One reader per payload concentrates all wire-format assumptions in one place and keeps the rest of the system working against its own model (typically a DTO).
tradeoffs: Silent data loss: a producer-side rename is indistinguishable from an intentional removal, and the reader quietly serves defaults instead of failing.
Tolerance covers additive change only; removed, retyped or semantically repurposed fields still break, and leniency can hide that they did.
Defaulting turns producer regressions into plausible but wrong data unless required fields still fail fast and loudly.
The discipline cannot be enforced by structure: a second ad-hoc read of the same payload elsewhere silently recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
Verification shifts to consumer-driven contract tests, because no schema check will report that a consumed field stopped arriving.
Observability drops: ignored and defaulted data leaves no trace unless logging, metrics or contract tests are added deliberately.
Preserving unknown fields for round-trips costs memory and complexity (extension-data dictionaries, unknown-field sets, flatten maps).
Being liberal in what you accept is a recognised security hazard (over-posting, mass assignment, parser discrepancies), so tolerant reading must be separated from validation of untrusted input.

participants.responsibility: The one component that consumes the payload: selects the elements it needs by name or path, applies an explicit default for each optional element, and never enumerates the payload as a whole, so unknown data is never visited.
The in-memory form the reader produces; the rest of the system depends on this model rather than on the wire shape, which is what stops producer changes from propagating inward.
Owns and evolves the payload; adds fields and elements on its own schedule, expecting consumers to ignore anything they do not understand.
The reader plus its tests, published to the producer (consumer-driven contract), stating exactly which fields the consumer reads and which test data it must keep passing.
Uses only the normalised result; it never parses payloads itself and therefore never learns a wire format.

use_cases: Consuming a partner or public REST/JSON or SOAP/XML API whose provider adds fields and elements on its own release cycle.
Event or message consumers on a shared bus whose producers deploy independently (backward-compatible schema evolution).
Reading long-lived persisted documents - serialised snapshots, caches, export files - written by older versions of the same program.
Client SDKs generated from a provider schema: replace regeneration with a hand-written tolerant reader over the parts the client actually uses.
Web and mobile clients reading backend responses, where ignoring an added field is preferable to shipping a client update.
Integration with several upstream versions at once (migration windows, A/B deployments), where one reader must serve payloads of mixed vintage.

Apache Avro schema resolution: a reader schema ignores record fields the writer added that it does not declare, and populates a reader field the writer lacks from its declared default - signalling an error only where no default exists.

Protocol Buffers consumers: parsers skip tags they do not recognise and preserve those unknown fields for re-serialisation, so a service built against an older .proto keeps working when an upstream adds fields.

Kubernetes API clients: unknown-field handling is an explicit per-request policy (fieldValidation Ignore/Strict/Warn), letting older clients keep reading objects from newer API servers instead of failing on fields they predate.
avoid_when: The data is safety- or money-critical and unexpected fields must be rejected, not ignored: use strict validation against an explicit schema plus a deliberate versioning policy.
Producer and consumer are deployed together and can share a compiled contract (same repository, atomic release): strict binding and a code generator give stronger guarantees for less discipline.
Unknown fields are a bug indicator rather than benign evolution (machine-generated payloads, internal protocols): strict deserialisation with fail-fast is simpler than tolerance plus contract tests.
The payload feeds security-sensitive behaviour (mass assignment, over-posting, hidden-field injection): enumerate accepted fields and reject the rest.

The transport serialises language objects directly (Java native serialisation, live object graphs): replace the format with a versioned, self-describing one instead of trying to be tolerant inside it.
anti_patterns: Blind tolerance: parsing whatever happens to be convenient without stating the consumed subset, so nobody can tell which producer change breaks the consumer.
Leniency applied to semantics: treating a retyped, repurposed or newly required field as if it were merely absent, hiding a real breaking change behind defaults.
Reader sprawl: several ad-hoc payload reads scattered across the codebase, each free to invent its own assumptions about the wire format.
Using tolerant reading as a substitute for validation of untrusted input (over-posting, mass assignment, hidden-field injection).
Preserving every unknown field forever "just in case" with no consumer, no use and no retention rule (extension-data bloat).
design_principles: Robustness principle (Postel's law): be conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept.
Separation of concerns: all payload reading lives in one reader, and the rest of the system sees only the normalised result.
Minimal assumptions (least knowledge): depend only on the data you actually consume, not on the shape of the document that carries it.
Information hiding: the wire format never leaks past the boundary component.
Open/closed: producers extend payloads without forcing consumer edits, while breaking changes still demand an explicit versioning decision.
best_practices: Read the fields you need by name or path and ignore everything else; do not validate the whole document against a rigid schema when only a few fields matter.
Write down the consumed subset - reader plus tests - and publish it to the producer as a consumer-driven contract.
Give every optional field an explicit, documented default and distinguish "absent" from "empty" or "explicitly null" where the semantics differ.
Keep exactly one reader per payload and expose its DTO to the rest of the code.
Classify changes deliberately: additive fields are tolerable; removals, retypes, semantic reuse and newly required fields need a versioning path.
Log or measure when a consumed field is defaulted or missing, so silent drift shows up before it becomes a data-quality incident.
Validate required fields, types and bounds on the way in; tolerant reading is a contract strategy, not an input-validation strategy.
sources: Fowler, Tolerant Reader, martinfowler.com bliki (9 May 2011) - read only the elements you need, make minimum structural assumptions, wrap the payload in a DTO, and send the reader and its tests to the provider.
Daigneau, Service Design Patterns: Fundamental Design Solutions for SOAP/WSDL and RESTful Web Services (2012) - full pattern description referenced by Fowler's bliki entry.
